title: The turning year
translation: The way the seasons change gets to you, every single part of it. Everyone says autumn is the most moving season, and fair enough. But spring is the one that really lifts your heart.

The birds start to sound like spring, the sun gets soft, the grass comes up along the fences. Then the haze settles in, and just as the blossoms start to look ready, rain and wind come day after day and they're gone in a rush. Until the trees turn green, it's one worry after another.

Orange blossoms are famous for bringing back memories, but for me it's the scent of plum blossom that brings back the old days. Then there's the fresh yellow kerria and the hazy wisteria. So much you can't let go of.

Someone important once said that around the Buddha's birthday and the Kamo Festival, when the young leaves fill out the treetops and look so cool, that's when you feel the world most deeply and miss people most. He was right.

In early summer they hang irises from the eaves and plant out the rice, and the water rails knock in the night. How could you not feel a little lonely? In midsummer, white gourd flowers show up on some shabby house and smoke drifts from a fire to keep the mosquitoes off, and that's moving too. The summer purification is nice as well. And the Star Festival is lovely.

Then the nights slowly get colder, the geese come crying overhead, the lower leaves of the bush clover turn colour, the early rice is cut and laid out to dry. Autumn has more of this than any other season. And the morning after a big autumn storm is something else.

I know all this has been said already in The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book. That doesn't mean I can't say it again. Keeping what you think to yourself just leaves you feeling bloated. So I let the brush run. It's a pointless pastime, meant to be torn up and thrown away, and nobody's supposed to read it anyway.
Winter is hardly worse than autumn. One morning there are red leaves caught in the grass by the pond, white frost everywhere, and steam rising off the garden stream. Lovely.

At the very end of the year, when everyone's rushing around, it's more moving than ever. And the moon late in the month, cold and clear, which nobody looks at because it's supposed to be dreary? That sky is lonely.

The end-of-year Buddhist service at court and the messengers riding out with offerings to the imperial tombs are moving and solemn. All the court ceremonies pile up on top of getting ready for spring, and it's impressive to watch. I love the way the demon-chasing on New Year's Eve runs straight into the New Year's dawn prayers.

On the last night of the year, in the dark, people run around with torches until past midnight, banging on doors and shouting about who knows what, rushing about as if their feet don't touch the ground. Then, toward dawn, it finally goes quiet, and the last of the year feels lonely.
The custom of honouring the dead on the night they come back has died out in the city, but out in the east they still did it, and that moved me.
And so the sky gets light. It doesn't look any different from yesterday, but it feels completely new. Pine decorations line the avenue, bright and cheerful, and that's moving too.

literal: The changing of the seasons: in every thing it is moving.
Everyone seems to say that the feeling of things is greater in autumn, and that is so, but what lifts the heart even more is surely the scenery of spring.

The voices of birds too become especially spring-like, in the mild sunlight, from the time the grass sprouts by the fences, spring deepens a little and haze spreads everywhere, and just when the blossoms begin to show signs, at that very time rain and wind continue and they hastily scatter.
Until the green leaves come, in every way one only troubles one's heart.
Orange blossoms are famous for it, but it is still with the scent of plum that things of the past come back and are fondly remembered.
The kerria looking fresh, the wisteria looking hazy: there are many things that are hard to give up.

Someone of rank said that around the Buddha's birthday and the festival, when the treetops of young leaves grow thick and cool, the feeling of the world and the longing for people are greater, and that is indeed so.
In the fifth month, when they thatch with irises, when they plant out the rice seedlings, the knocking of the water rails and such: how could these not be lonely?
Around the sixth month, at a humble house, the evening-face flowers showing white, and a mosquito-smudge fire smouldering, is also moving.
The sixth-month purification is also delightful.
Celebrating Tanabata is graceful.

As the nights gradually grow cold, when the geese come crying, when the lower leaves of the bush clover colour, cutting and drying the early rice fields and so on: the gathered things are most numerous in autumn.
And the morning after an autumn storm is delightful.
If I go on saying these things, they have all grown old in the Tale of Genji, the Pillow Book and so on, but it is not that I will not say the same things again now.
Since not saying what one thinks is a thing that swells the belly, I let my brush go, and since these are idle amusements to be torn up and thrown away, they are not something people should see.
Now, the scenery of winter's withering is surely hardly inferior to autumn.
On a morning when red leaves have fallen and stopped in the grass at the water's edge, and frost lies very white, the mist rising from the garden stream is delightful.
The time when the year has completely ended and everyone hurries together is incomparably moving.
The sky of the twentieth-and-more days, with the moon cold and clear, which no one looks at because it is considered dreary, is lonely.
The Buddha-names service and the dispatching of the messengers with the first offerings are moving and noble.
The many public ceremonies, piled on top of the preparations for spring, and the way they are held: that is splendid.
That the demon-chasing continues into the prayer to the four directions is delightful.

On the last night, very dark, lighting torches, until past midnight, people run around knocking on people's gates, shouting grandly about who knows what, hurrying as if their feet were in the air; and that from dawn on, as one would expect, it becomes quiet: that makes the last of the year lonely.
The custom of honouring the spirits on the night the dead come, which is not done in the capital these days, was still done in the eastern provinces, and that was moving.
So the look of the dawning sky does not seem changed from yesterday, but there is a feeling of everything being new.
The look of the avenues, with pines set up all along them, bright and happy, is also moving.

notes.quote: 物の哀れは秋こそまされと
notes.text: In Japanese poetry, autumn was the season of {物|もの}の{哀|あは}れ, the feeling that things pass. Kenkō agrees and then sets spring against it: a small argument with tradition in the first lines.

notes.quote: 花橘は名にこそおへれ
notes.text: The orange blossom ({花橘|はなたちばな}) is 'famous' because of a classic Kokinshū poem: its scent brings back the sleeves of someone you once loved. Kenkō says plum does it for him. こそ … おへれ, then a comma: 'although', as in section 1.

{灌仏|くわんぶつ}: the Buddha's birthday, the eighth day of the fourth month. {祭|まつり}: the Kamo Festival in the same month (see section 137). おほせられし: 'said', with respect, so the speaker was someone of high rank.
The call of the water rail ({水鶏|くひな}) sounds like knocking on a door, so poets wrote that it 'knocks'. In love poetry, a knock at night could be a lover, or just the bird.
{夕顔|ゆふがほ}: the white flowers of the bottle gourd, which open in the evening. Readers would think of the Yūgao chapter of the Tale of Genji, where a flower on a poor house begins a love story.

{野分|のわき}: 'the field divider', a strong autumn storm. Sei Shōnagon has a whole section on the morning after one, and so does Genji. Kenkō knows it, which is why the next sentence says all this has been written before.

notes.quote: おぼしき事云はぬは腹ふくるるわざなれば
notes.text: 'Not saying what you think makes your belly swell': an old saying, found in the Ōkagami. Here Kenkō explains, in the middle of the seasons, why he writes at all. He calls it a pointless pastime, as in the preface.

{御仏名|おぶつみやう}: a court service at the end of the year where the names of thousands of Buddhas were recited to wipe out the year's sins. {荷前|のさき}: offerings of the first tribute of the year, sent to the imperial tombs.
{追儺|ついな}: chasing out demons on the last night of the year, the ancestor of today's setsubun. {四方拝|しはうはい}: the emperor's prayer to the four directions at dawn on New Year's Day.

notes.quote: 亡き人のくる夜とて魂まつるわざ
notes.text: An old belief that the dead visited at the end of the year. Later, the visit of the dead was linked only with the summer Obon festival. あはれなりしか: し, しか from き, so Kenkō saw it himself in the east, where he had spent time.
Pine decorations at the gates for New Year, the ancestors of today's {門松|かどまつ}. The section ends where it began: everything changes, and the change itself is what moves him.
